A cellist plays a sonata with his eyes shut while a library audience sits through a mistake
A page turner is corrected for reading ahead of the pianist and learns to stay a line behind the piano

item.passage:
Mrs. Adair, her flute teacher, had asked Priya on Monday, and by Saturday Priya had read the instructions so many times that she could have recited them. Stand when Ms. Okafor nods. Turn from the top corner. Sit down. Keep your hands in your lap and your eyes on the music, one line behind the piano, never ahead.

The recital was in the reading room of the public library, with the shelves pushed back and sixty folding chairs set out in rows. Ms. Okafor was the pianist, and a cellist named Mr. Brandt was the soloist. Priya, who had never turned a page for anyone, sat on a low stool at the pianist's left elbow.

The first piece went the way the instructions said it would. Ms. Okafor tipped her head a fraction of an inch at the bottom of each page, Priya stood and turned and sat, and the music went on as if the paper had simply been waiting for her.

The second piece was a sonata in three movements, and halfway through the slow one, Priya's fingers came away with two pages instead of one. She saw it at once: the next page began with a crowd of notes where there should have been a long held chord. Her face went hot. She pried at the corner, lost it, found it, and folded the extra page back, and by the time the right page lay open Ms. Okafor was three lines down it.

The piano had kept going the whole time. Priya had heard a pause, she was sure of it, but when she looked up, the cellist was playing with his eyes shut, and nobody in the sixty chairs had moved.

Afterward, while people stood in line for lemonade, Priya found Ms. Okafor packing her music into a canvas bag and began to apologize. Ms. Okafor took the sonata back out, opened it to the slow movement, and ran a thumbnail between the two pages. They came apart with a small dry sound. There was a pale brown ring where they had touched.

"Tea," Ms. Okafor said. "From a rehearsal two winters ago. I should have checked them this morning. That one was mine."

"But you kept playing," Priya said. "You were past the bottom of the page before I even found it."

"I learned that movement by heart in March."

Priya looked at the open book. "Then why bring the music at all?"

Ms. Okafor smiled and slid it back into the bag. "Because the night I leave it at home will be the night my memory decides to take a holiday. The book is there so that I can forget it's there." She buckled the bag. "Mrs. Adair says you're free in December. There's a Brahms trio, and the pages in that one are clean."

Priya walked out past the lemonade table without taking any. She was already thinking about the top corner, and about how lightly she would have to hold it.

It comes up twenty yards from where it went down,
as if the harbor had moved it while I blinked,
only the neck and the hooked bill showing,
the rest of it riding low, a log with ideas.

A fish goes in headfirst, still working,
a silver thumb the throat takes in one swallow,
and the bird looks round at the gulls on the breakwater
the way a man looks round after a sneeze.

Then it hauls itself onto the piling by the fuel dock,
wingbeats and claws and a scrabble of wet feet,
and settles, and opens its wings to the wind
like someone hanging up a coat that has been in the rain.

I laughed the first morning. It looked like an umbrella
blown inside out and left on a post,
a black thing broken at every joint,
holding a pose it had forgotten to drop.

But the ducks go home dry, and this one cannot.
Its feathers take the water in, the man
who rents the kayaks told me, so it sinks
more easily, and chases deeper, and pays for it after.

So every morning it stands there twenty minutes,
half an hour, shifting a little when the wind shifts,
while the air goes through its feathers
the way a comb goes through a child's wet hair.

The kayaks go out. The fuel truck comes and goes.
A gull lands on the next piling and leaves again.
The bird keeps its arms out through all of it,
as patient as laundry on a line.

I come down at seven with my coffee now
and look for it first, before the boats,
before the weather. Some days it is already there,
arms wide, drying, getting ready to be wet again.

The summer I turned sixteen, the county paid me nine dollars an hour to sit in a folding chair at the corner of Route 9 and Haller Road and count everything that went by.

The equipment was a board the size of a cafeteria tray with twelve metal counters screwed to it in four rows, one row for each direction a car could come from, and in each row one counter for left, one for straight and one for right. Every time a vehicle passed through the intersection, I pressed the button that matched where it had come from and where it went. The engineer who trained me, a tall woman named Ms. Vance, made me practice on photographs for an hour before she let me near the road. "Turns are the whole point," she said. "Anybody can count cars."

I worked from seven to seven for ten days, with a relief counter, a college student named Dev, who took over for half an hour at noon and again at four. Before 1871, buying a length of cloth in Corran Falls was a contest. No price was written anywhere in the town's three dry-goods stores. A customer pointed at a fabric, the clerk named a figure, and the two of them bargained until one gave way.

The system rewarded a particular kind of shopper. A farmer's wife who had bargained every week for twenty years, and who knew to the penny what the store had paid its supplier, could walk out with calico at a price a newcomer would never be offered. The newcomer, the shy, and the children sent with a coin and a list paid more, sometimes much more, for the same yard of the same cloth. Clerks, for their part, were hired as much for their nerve as for their arithmetic.

In the spring of 1871, Hester Lyle opened a fourth store on Bridge Street and hung a small card from every bolt and every box. Each card carried a price in ink. A sign over the counter read ONE PRICE TO ALL, and Lyle's clerks were told to answer any lower offer with the same sentence: "The price is on the card."

The town's first response was to stay away. Experienced bargainers took the cards as an insult, a way of telling them that their skill was worth nothing at Lyle's. A letter to the Corran Falls Courier called the store "a place where a customer is permitted to agree." For most of that first year, Lyle's counter was quiet on the days when the others were crowded.

The customers who did come were, at first, mostly the ones the old system had served worst. Mothers sent children to Lyle's because a child would pay what the card said and nothing more. Families new to the valley came because they could see a price before they had to speak. Lyle also found that she could train a clerk in a week, because the job now required only measuring, adding and wrapping.

By 1874 the store on Bridge Street was the busiest in town. The other three held out for a time, then began, one after another, to hang cards of their own. The last of them gave in around 1880, though its owner was said to bargain privately with a few old customers until he retired.

The cards did more than speed up the counter. Under the old system, a price had been a private agreement between two people, and nobody could say for certain what anyone else had paid. Once the price hung on the bolt, it became a public fact. A customer could compare Lyle's calico with a rival's without bargaining for either, and a store that charged too much could be seen doing it.

Dodder looks less like a plant than like a spill of orange string. Its thin stems wind over clover, alfalfa, tomatoes and many other plants, and along them grow only tiny scales where leaves would be. Most of the more than one hundred species of dodder make little or none of their own food. Instead, a dodder lives on other plants, drawing water and sugar out of their stems.

That way of life gives a dodder seedling an unusual problem. It sprouts from a seed in the soil as a pale, leafless thread, and it has only the food stored in the seed to live on. If it does not reach a suitable plant within several days, it dies. As it grows, its tip sweeps slowly in circles, as the growing tips of many climbing plants do, and the circling may help it brush against whatever stands nearby.

For a long time, it was unclear whether a seedling found a host by chance or by some kind of sense. In the mid-2000s, a team of plant scientists set out to test the question. They planted dodder seedlings a short distance from young tomato plants, and most of the seedlings grew toward the tomatoes. When the scientists replaced the tomato plant with a vial holding an extract of the chemicals that tomato plants release into the air, the seedlings bent toward the vial. Seedlings beside a vial of plain solvent grew in no particular direction.

The seedlings also seemed to choose. Offered a tomato plant on one side and a wheat plant on the other, they grew toward the tomato more often. The researchers reported that at least one chemical in wheat's scent appeared to steer seedlings away. Grasses such as wheat are generally poor hosts for this kind of dodder, and the seedlings behave as if they can tell the difference from a distance.

Once its tip touches a suitable stem, a dodder coils around it and grows small pegs that push into the host's tissue and tap the tubes that carry water and sugar. Its own root soon withers. From then on the vine has no connection to the soil, and it depends on its hosts, sending new stems from plant to plant. In a field of alfalfa or tomatoes, a single dodder can end up draining many plants, and farmers treat it as a serious weed.

It is tempting to say that a dodder seedling smells its way to dinner. A seedling lacks a nose and nerves, though. What it has is a growing tip that responds to particular chemicals in the air, bending toward some and away from others.
